'''Benjamin Abeles''' (23 June 1925 – 14 December 2020)<ref>{{cite web |last1=Abeles |first1=David |title=Benjamin Abeles obituary |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2021/mar/21/benjamin-abeles-obituary |website=The Guardian |date=21 March 2021}}</ref> was an Austrian-Czech physicist whose research in the 1960s in the US on [[germanium]]–[[silicon]] [[alloy]]s led to the technology used to power space probes such as the [[Voyager spacecraft|''Voyager'' spacecraft]]. He grew up in Austria and Czechoslovakia and arrived in the UK in 1939 on one of the ''[[Kindertransport]]'' missions. He completed his education after the war in Czechoslovakia and Israel (from 1949), obtaining a doctorate in physics. He then lived and worked as a research physicist in the US and retired in 1995. His honours include the 1979 [[Stuart Ballantine Medal]] and his induction into the [[New Jersey Inventors Hall of Fame]] (1991).

==Early life and education==
Born in [[Vienna]] in 1925 as Bedrich Abeles, to an [[Ashkenazi Jewish]] family. His mother Selma was of [[Austrian Jewish]] origins. Abele's father, Ernst, came from a well-to-do [[Czech Jewish]] family. Abeles lived in [[Czechoslovakia]] from 1934.<ref name="lidovky">{{cite web|url=http://www.lidovky.cz/wintonovo-dite-vyvinulo-zdroj-energie-pro-kosmicke-sondy-pnm-/veda.aspx?c=A110126_095908_ln_veda_jmt|title=Wintonovo dítě vyvinulo zdroj energie pro kosmické sondy|date=26 January 2011|publisher=lidovky.cz|access-date=16 August 2013}}</ref> In July 1939, aged 14, he was one of hundreds of Jewish children brought from [[Prague]] to London through the efforts of British humanitarian [[Nicholas Winton]], an example of the various ''[[Kindertransport]]'' missions that saved many such children from the impending dangers of World War II and the Holocaust.<ref name="lidovky"/> His parents and older sister were later deported and murdered by the Nazis.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1 February 2018|title=Child refugees who fled Nazis plead for UK to take in more migrants|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-42906314|access-date=16 December 2020}}</ref> At age 15, he worked as a waiter and took correspondence courses in English, mathematics, physics and chemistry.  When he was 18, Abeles served as a mechanic in the war as part of [[No. 311 Squadron RAF]].<ref name="lidovky"/> He then returned to Czechoslovakia after the war and studied at [[Charles University in Prague]] and [[Czech Technical University in Prague]], before moving to Israel in 1949 to study for his physics doctorate in Jerusalem.<ref name="lidovky"/> His thesis, published in 1955, was titled 'The Galvanomagnetic Effects in Bismuth and Bi–Sn Alloys'.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://lib-phds1.weizmann.ac.il/vufind/Record/000074538/Details#tabnav|title=התופעות הגלונומגנטיות בביסמוט ונתכי ביסמוט-בדיל|publisher=Weizmann Institute of Science|access-date=17 August 2013|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304002154/http://lib-phds1.weizmann.ac.il/vufind/Record/000074538/Details#tabnav|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Career==
Following the award of his PhD, Abeles worked in Israel on germanium electronics before moving to the United States to carry out research in Princeton for the [[Radio Corporation of America]].<ref name="lidovky"/> During his career, Abeles worked at both the [[David Sarnoff Research Center]] and at Exxon Research and Engineering in [[Annandale, New Jersey|Annandale]], New Jersey. Working with George D. Cody in the 1960s, Abeles developed germanium–silicon alloys that were used in the development of the [[radioisotope thermoelectric generator]]s used to power spacecraft and probes engaged in long voyages of [[space exploration]].<ref name="NJHOF"/> Abeles also worked as a professor at the [[University of Texas]].<ref name="lidovky"/>

==Recognition and later life==
For their work, Abeles and Cody received the 1979 [[Stuart Ballantine Medal]] (Engineering) from the Franklin Institute,<ref>{{cite web|title=Franklin Laureate Database: Benjamin Abeles|publisher=Franklin Institute|url=http://www.fi.edu/winners/detail.faw?winner_id=2177|access-date=16 August 2013|archive-date=22 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120222143743/http://www.fi.edu/winners/detail.faw?winner_id=2177|url-status=dead}}</ref> and were inducted into the [[New Jersey Inventors Hall of Fame]] in 1991.<ref name="NJHOF">{{cite web|url=http://www.njinvent.org/awards/Awards91.html|title=1991 Award Winners|publisher=New Jersey Inventors Hall of Fame|access-date=16 August 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160228100151/http://www.njinvent.org/awards/Awards91.html|archive-date=28 February 2016}}</ref> Abeles's 65th birthday in 1990 was marked by a symposium in his honour: 'Physical Phenomena in Granular Materials'.<ref>{{cite web |title=Physical phenomena in granular materials: symposium held April 16–20, 1990, San Francisco, California, U.S.A |website=WorldCat |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/489910429 |oclc=489910429}}</ref> He retired in 1995, and subsequently lived predominantly in the UK.<ref name="lidovky"/>

Abeles died in [[Leicester]], England on 14 December 2020, aged 95.<ref>[https://www.idnes.cz/technet/veda/benjamin-abeles-fyzik-raf.A201214_192614_veda_pka Zemřel fyzik Bedřich Abeles. Sloužil v RAF, vynalezl pohon pro Voyager] {{LL|cs}}</ref>
